notes.subtitle: Place Value, Terminating Decimals & Everyday Measures

concepts.title: Decimal place value
concepts.text: Digits to the right of the decimal point represent tenths, hundredths, thousandths and successively smaller parts.

concepts.title: Comparing decimals
concepts.text: Write trailing zeros so the decimals have equal places, then compare from the greatest place to the smallest.

concepts.title: Fractions and decimals
concepts.text: A decimal fraction has denominator 10, 100, 1,000 and so on. Convert only fractions with terminating decimal forms in this chapter.

concepts.title: Operations in context
concepts.text: Align decimal points for addition and subtraction, and express money, mass, length or temperature in one unit before operating.

formulas: Digit value = digit × value of its place
a/10ⁿ gives a decimal with n decimal places after necessary zero padding
Appending trailing zeros does not change a decimal’s value
₹1 = 100 paise
method: Convert all quantities to the same unit.
Write decimals with their decimal points vertically aligned.
Add trailing zeros where needed, then add or subtract by place value.
Check the size, unit and decimal placement of the answer.

example.question: A parcel weighs 3 kg 450 g. After removing 1 kg 875 g, what mass remains?
steps: Write the masses as 3.450 kg and 1.875 kg.

From ₹200, subtract ₹68.75 and ₹49.90.
A temperature of 15.8°C rises by 4.65°C and falls by 7.3°C.

tips: Align decimal points, not the last digits.
A longer decimal is not automatically a larger number.
Retain unit zeros during working so that each place remains clear.

notes.subtitle: Comparisons, Equivalent Ratios & Proportions

concepts.title: Ratio versus fraction
concepts.text: A fraction commonly names part of one whole; a ratio compares two quantities in a stated order. A ratio can be greater than 1.

concepts.title: Like units and simplest form
concepts.text: Convert both quantities to the same unit, then divide both terms by their HCF.

concepts.title: Equivalent ratios
concepts.text: Multiplying or dividing both terms by the same non-zero number preserves the comparison.

concepts.title: Proportion
concepts.text: Two equal ratios form a proportion. The product of the extremes equals the product of the means.

formulas: a:b = a/b
a:b = ka:kb for k ≠ 0
If a:b = c:d, then ad = bc
For ratio m:n, total parts = m + n
method: Keep the quantities in the order named in the question.
Convert both quantities to the same unit.
Simplify by the HCF or form an equivalent ratio using one common factor.
For a proportion, verify that the cross-products are equal.

practice.question: Reduce 72:108 to simplest form.

Check whether 8, 12, 14 and 21 are in proportion.

If A:B = 2:5 and B:C = 10:7, find A:B:C.

tips: Order matters: a:b is generally not b:a.
Never compare measurements in different units.
Equal cross-products are a reliable final check for a proportion.

notes.subtitle: Parts per Hundred & Direct Rates

concepts.title: Meaning of percent
concepts.text: Percent means per hundred. Thus p% represents p parts out of every 100 equal parts.

concepts.title: Converting forms
concepts.text: Write a percentage over 100 to obtain a fraction; rewrite a simple fraction with denominator 100 to obtain a percentage.

concepts.title: Percentage of a quantity
concepts.text: To find p% of a quantity, multiply the quantity by p/100 and simplify before multiplying when possible.

concepts.title: Direct unitary method
concepts.text: When more identical items give a proportionally larger total, first find the value of one item and then the value of the required number.

formulas: p% of Q=(p/100)×Q
a/b as a percent=(a/b)×100%
Value of 1 unit=total value÷number of units
Value of required units=value of 1 unit×required units
method: Identify whether the question asks for a percentage or a direct rate.
For percentage, write the percent as a fraction over 100.
For unitary method, divide to find the value of one unit.
Multiply by the required quantity and check that the direction is sensible.

example.question: Twelve books cost ₹300. Find the cost of 7 books, then find 20% of that cost.
example.answer: Seven books cost ₹175, and 20% of this cost is ₹35.

practice.question: Write 32% as a fraction in simplest form.

Find 15% of 300.

Five kilograms of apples cost ₹400. Find the cost of 8 kg.
In a group of 240 children, 35% choose chess. How many choose chess?

tips: The symbol % already includes division by 100.
In direct unitary problems, find one unit before scaling up.
Use estimation: a small percentage should be a smaller part of the whole.

notes.subtitle: Simple Motion & Consistent Units

concepts.title: Speed
concepts.text: Speed tells how much distance is covered in one unit of time. A greater speed means more distance in the same time.

concepts.title: Distance
concepts.text: At a fixed speed, distance increases directly with travel time.

concepts.title: Time
concepts.text: Travel time is found by dividing the distance by the speed when both use matching units.

concepts.title: Units
concepts.text: Use compatible units before applying a formula: hours with km/h and minutes with m/min, for example.

formulas: Speed=distance÷time
Distance=speed×time
Time=distance÷speed
1 hour=60 minutes
method: Write the known distance, speed and time with units.
Convert time or distance so the units are compatible.
Choose the formula containing the required quantity.
Calculate and write the correct unit with the answer.

tips: Never combine minutes directly with a speed given per hour.
Speed needs a distance unit divided by a time unit.
Check whether a faster speed or longer time should make the distance larger.

notes.subtitle: Variables, Terms, Patterns & Evaluation

concepts.title: Language of algebra
concepts.text: A constant has a fixed value, a variable can take different values, and an unknown is a value to be found. An expression combines numbers, variables and operations without an equality sign.

concepts.title: Terms, factors and coefficients
concepts.text: Terms are separated by + or − signs. Each term is a product of factors; its numerical factor is the coefficient, while a term without a variable is the constant term.

concepts.title: Polynomials and degree
concepts.text: A polynomial with one term is a monomial, with two terms a binomial, and with three terms a trinomial; polynomials may also have more than three terms. Its degree is the greatest exponent of its variable with a non-zero coefficient.

concepts.title: Patterns and substitution
concepts.text: A variable can express a rule that works for every position in a pattern. To evaluate an expression, replace each variable by its given value and follow the order of operations.

formulas: A term = numerical coefficient × variable factor(s)
Degree of axⁿ = n, where a ≠ 0
Arithmetic pattern term = first term + (n − 1) × common increase
Perimeter of a square of side s = 4s
Perimeter of a rectangle = 2(l + b)
method: Separate the expression into terms, keeping each term’s sign.
Identify the variable factors, coefficients and constant term.
Translate each phrase into the required algebraic operation, or substitute the stated variable values.
Use the order of operations and check that the final value matches the context.

example.question: A hall has r rows of 18 chairs and 12 extra chairs at the front. Frame an expression for the total and evaluate it for r = 9.
steps: The r equal rows contain 18r chairs.
Add the 12 extra chairs to get 18r + 12.
example.answer: The expression is 18r + 12, and the hall has 174 chairs when r = 9.

practice.question: State the coefficient of x and the constant term in −8x + 11.
Which term is like 5a²: −3a², 5a or 5b²?
List the terms and numerical coefficients in 9p + 2q + 3.
practice.answer: Terms: 9p, 2q, 3; coefficients of p and q: 9 and 2; constant term: 3.

practice.question: Evaluate 2m² − n for m = 3 and n = 4.
Write the nth term of 7, 12, 17, 22, … .
A cinema ticket costs ₹t. Frame and evaluate the cost of 4 tickets plus a booking charge of ₹20 when t = 85.

tips: A minus sign belongs to the term that follows it.
Terms are like only when every variable and exponent matches.
Use brackets when substituting a negative value.

notes.subtitle: Balancing, Solving & Verifying One-Variable Equations

concepts.title: Expression versus equation
concepts.text: An expression has no equality sign. An equation states that two expressions are equal, and its solution is the value that makes this statement true.

concepts.title: The balance principle
concepts.text: An equation stays balanced when the same valid operation is performed on both sides; any divisor used must be non-zero. Use inverse operations to isolate the variable.

concepts.title: Forming an equation
concepts.text: Choose a variable for the unknown, translate the words into an expression, and use the given total or comparison to form an equality.

concepts.title: Verification
concepts.text: Substitute the proposed solution into the original equation. It is correct only when the left-hand side and right-hand side have the same value.

formulas: x + a = b ⟹ x = b − a
x − a = b ⟹ x = b + a
ax = b ⟹ x = b ÷ a, a ≠ 0
x ÷ a = b ⟹ x = ab, a ≠ 0
Do the same operation to both sides of an equation
method: Choose a variable and form the equation from the given information.
Undo addition or subtraction first using the same operation on both sides.
Undo multiplication or division to isolate the variable.
Substitute the answer into the original equation and confirm both sides are equal.

example.question: A taxi charges ₹40 as a fixed fee and ₹12 per kilometre. A journey costs ₹112. How many kilometres were travelled?
steps: Let the distance be d km.

practice.question: Solve x + 13 = 31.
Solve y − 8 = 17.
Solve 6m = 54.
Solve p ÷ 7 = 5.
Solve 3n + 5 = 26 and verify.
Four identical pens and a ₹10 notebook cost ₹74. Form an equation and find the cost of one pen.

tips: Keep the variable term unchanged until its added or subtracted constant is removed.
Never perform an operation on only one side of an equation.
Verify in the original equation, not in a rearranged line.
